intro: Until now this course has looked at the Qur'an from a distance: what the book is, how it is arranged, where it came from, what it teaches. This unit sits down with the text itself. You will read whole surahs, slowly, the way a commentator or a literature class reads: verse by verse, noticing the sound, the structure, the speaker, and what each line does. The surahs chosen are all ones that Muslim tradition dates to Mecca, before 622, when the community was small and the message was mostly about one God, judgment and care for the weak.

The first chapter reads five short surahs that Muslims hear every day in prayer: Al-Fatiha, the opening; Al-'Alaq, which tradition calls the first revelation; Ad-Duha and Al-'Asr; and Al-Ikhlas, four verses on the oneness of God. The second chapter reads two long narrative surahs, Yusuf and Maryam, and sets them beside Genesis and the Gospel of Luke. You will hear from classical commentators such as al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, from Sufi poets, and from academic scholars, and you will compare public-domain translations.

By the end you will be able to read a surah as a unit of meaning, find where it turns, name the tools of Meccan style and Qur'anic storytelling, and explain how Muslim and academic readers ask different questions of the same text. You will practice saying "the Qur'an says" and "Muslims believe" and "al-Tabari reads this as," and you will write an argument from the text with the verses cited.
bigQuestion: What does a Meccan surah do, line by line, and how do its readers, Muslim and academic, unpack it?

timeline.t: Muslim tradition: the first verses, 96:1-5, come to Muhammad in a cave on Mount Hira
The earliest Meccan surahs, short and rhymed, including Ad-Duha, Al-'Asr and Al-Ikhlas by the traditional order
Muslim tradition: some Muslims flee to Abyssinia; Ja'far recites from Surah Maryam before the king
Some commentators place Surah Yusuf in a hard year after the deaths of Khadija and Abu Talib
The migration to Medina; surahs from this point on are called Medinan
Muslim tradition: a standard written copy of the Qur'an is made under the caliph Uthman
Death of al-Tabari, whose commentary gathers early readings of every verse
Death of Ibn Kathir, whose commentary explains the Qur'an by the Qur'an and hadith
Death of Jami, Persian poet of Yusuf and Zulaykha, a Sufi reading of Surah 12
George Sale publishes the first English translation made directly from Arabic
The Egyptian standard edition of the Qur'an is printed in Cairo, with a traditional order of revelation
Marmaduke Pickthall publishes The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, this course's text

words.d: "The Opening," the seven-verse first surah, recited in every unit of Muslim prayer
commentary on the Qur'an; al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir wrote major works of tafsir
a surah that tradition dates before 622; usually short, rhymed, with oaths and warnings of judgment
rhymed prose, the style of many Meccan surahs, built for the ear rather than fixed meter
a solemn swearing by something, such as the morning or the declining day, that opens many Meccan surahs
the belief that God is one, without partner, parent or child; stated in Surah 112
patience or endurance; named in Al-'Asr and shown by Ya'qub in Surah 12
the arrangement or coherence of a surah as a whole with a central theme
verses at the start and end of a story that say why it is told, as in 12:3 and 12:111
pointing to a known story without telling it in full; the Qur'an's usual way with earlier scripture
a line that returns at intervals, such as "make mention in the Scripture of" in Surah 19
stories from Jewish and Christian sources used by some commentators; Ibn Kathir warned against them

test.q: Which surah is recited in every unit of the Muslim daily prayer?
test.why: Al-Fatiha is part of every rak'ah; a hadith in Bukhari and Muslim says a prayer without it is incomplete.

test.q: What word begins the verses that tradition calls the first revelation?
test.why: 96:1 begins "Read" (iqra'); "Say" opens Al-Ikhlas and "Praise" opens Al-Fatiha's second verse.

test.q: Which surah joins memory to duty with the word "Therefor"?
test.why: Ad-Duha, 93:9-11, turns the memory of being an orphan into a command not to oppress the orphan.

test.q: In Al-'Asr, who is excepted from loss?
choices: those who recite the whole Qur'an
those who believe, do good, and urge one another to truth and patience
test.why: 103:3 gives four parts: faith, good works, exhorting to truth, exhorting to endurance.

test.q: What does Al-Ikhlas deny about God?
choices: that God has children or a parent or any equal
test.why: 112:3-4 say God begets not, was not begotten, and has none comparable; this is the surah's statement of tawhid.

test.q: Which translation may be quoted in this course because it is public domain?
test.why: Pickthall's 1930 translation is public domain in the United States; Yusuf Ali and Arberry are not.

test.q: Which feature marks a surah as Meccan in style?
choices: short rhymed verses with oaths and images of judgment
test.why: Meccan surahs are short, rhythmic and concerned with one God, judgment and the weak; law belongs to Medinan surahs.

test.q: What is the traditional place of Surah 96 in the order of revelation printed in the 1924 Cairo edition?
test.why: The Cairo chronology places Al-'Alaq first; Al-Fatiha is fifth and Al-Ikhlas twenty-second.

test.q: What does Surah 12 call the story of Yusuf?
test.why: 12:3, in Pickthall, says "the best of narratives"; the other phrases belong to Al-Fatiha and Surah 19.

test.q: What object returns three times in Surah 12 as a lie, a proof and a healing?
test.why: The shirt bears false blood (12:18), is torn from behind (12:28), and restores Ya'qub's sight (12:96).

test.q: Which detail is in Genesis but not in Surah 12?
choices: the names of the brothers and the coat of many colors
test.why: The Qur'an names no brothers and has no coat; it assumes hearers know the outline and keeps what the lesson needs.

test.q: What sign is Zakariya given in Surah 19?
test.why: 19:10 gives three nights of silence while sound of body; the stream and dates belong to Maryam's scene.

test.q: Who speaks in Maryam's defense when her people accuse her?
choices: the visitor who brought the news
test.why: In 19:29-33 Maryam points to the child and the infant Isa speaks, calling himself God's servant and prophet.

test.q: What is allusion in Qur'anic narrative?
choices: rhyme at the end of each verse
telling part of a story the audience already knows
test.why: The Qur'an points to known stories and tells the part it needs, dropping names, places and dates.

test.q: A Sufi poet reads Yusuf's story as the soul's longing for God; an academic scholar dates Surah 12 and compares it to Genesis. What is true of both?
choices: Both prove the story is fiction
Both ask questions of the same text without settling whether it is revealed
test.why: Sufi, classical and academic readers ask different questions of one text; none of these questions decides the religious claim.

write.prompt: How does a Meccan surah turn a small text into a large idea? Choose one short surah from chapter 23 and one scene from Surah 12 or 19. Cite at least two passages by surah and verse, quote Pickthall (1930) where you can, and explain what each passage says and how at least two readers, such as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, a Sufi poet or an academic scholar, have read it.
tips: Name every text you cite by surah and verse, and name the translation and its year.
Attribute every belief: "Muslims believe," "the Qur'an says," "al-Tabari reads this as," "Neuwirth argues."
Find the turning point of the surah or scene and explain what changes there.
Compare readings rather than ranking them; show what question each reader is asking.
Use the unit's terms, such as oath, saj', frame, refrain and allusion, and explain each the first time.
